blocks.text: Autogirl has gone roughly seven years without a disclosed institutional round. Arinze planned a seed round in 2022, but we found no record of it closing; the 2022–2024 funding downturn and cooling investor appetite for Nigerian mobility may have contributed. The company stayed largely revenue-funded through its Ghana expansion. Whether the delay was a choice or a round that failed to close is not public.

blocks.lead: Instrument choice and debt vs. equity.
blocks.text: Autogirl’s main financing instrument is its marketplace: owners carry the vehicles, and by 2024 had received more than $530,000 from an asset base Autogirl never financed (TechCabal, January 2026). Moove offers a contrast. It financed ride-hailing drivers’ cars, with repayment linked to their platform earnings, and announced the end of its Nigerian operations about a month after Uber left Nigeria in September 2026, transferring vehicles valued at about ₦35bn to customers at no further cost (Nairametrics, October 2026; Nation Africa, 2026). Moove gave no reason, drivers could still work on other platforms such as Bolt, and Moove continues to raise capital elsewhere, so the link to Uber’s exit is a plausible explanation rather than an established cause. Autogirl had no fleet debt to unwind. Risk remains: a ₦20M crash showed that when an owner’s insurance fails, Autogirl becomes the insurer of last resort. Verified insurance, guarantors and tracker-backed KYC now do the work a reserve or debt facility would do elsewhere.

blocks.label: Company-reported
blocks.text: Company materials for the Prado investment offer cite 520+ vehicles, 20,000+ rentals and ₦2B+ paid to owners, and the company website cites 70,000+ rides; these figures are company-reported and use different bases.

Company materials describe a Prado investment opportunity that raises outside capital on the strength of Prado rental returns. Its classification cannot be established from public sources, so this study does not treat it as equity. Classification depends on structure: shares in Autogirl would make it dilutive equity; investor-owned vehicles managed by Autogirl would make it off-balance-sheet asset capital; a promised fixed return would make it debt-like whatever the label. Company marketing to car owners describes earnings of up to ₦30M a year as “guaranteed” (Muvment by Autogirl, July 2026); if similar language applies to investors, Autogirl would carry the return risk, and a pooled, return-promising scheme may raise questions under the Investments and Securities Act 2025. The amount raised, investor and vehicle numbers, instrument and any return guarantee are not public.

blocks.text: Disclosed external money has come only from an accelerator programme run by a trust and a grant for women founders, neither taking equity or a board seat. Arinze has said she aims to sell Muvment to a global peer-to-peer platform such as Turo when it enters Africa (TechCabal, January 2026); a moderate-valuation trade sale suits angels, strategic and impact investors better than a venture fund needing a much larger outcome.
The founding team (Arinze and COO Ebuka Arinze) is reported to hold the company in full; whether the Prado offer changes this is not public.

Revenue, costs and owner payouts are in naira and now cedis. With no dollar liabilities, Autogirl avoids the currency mismatch facing dollar-funded peers, but has no hard-currency buffer for cross-border growth. No follow-on institutional funding has been disclosed.

why: Chinazom Arinze started Autogirl with no capital. As a law student, she sold cars on commission, flipped her first car with the proceeds and organised campus-to-Lagos rides. Car trading tied up too much cash for too little margin, so she moved into rentals, matching corporate clients who needed cars for three to twelve months with private cars sitting idle between commutes: owners list vehicles, and Autogirl supplies customers, drivers and verification. By her account, revenue covered all staff costs by 2022 with no outside investor (Nairametrics, June 2022), and the company has since entered Ghana. Because owners finance the fleet, the model does the work capital does elsewhere, making Autogirl a foil to Sendy and to Moove, the Lagos-founded vehicle financier that announced the end of its Nigerian operations in October 2026, a month after Uber left the market (Nairametrics, October 2026).
lessons: In mobility, a marketplace that lets owners fund the fleet can substitute for capital: Autogirl entered a second country with no disclosed vehicle financing.
Asset-light moves risk; it does not remove it. Insurance, guarantor and KYC terms in the host and rental contracts are the real risk controls and have to be enforced from day one.

Asset-linked raises need careful classification. A raise built around one vehicle type can be equity, asset finance or debt depending on who holds title and carries the return risk, which determines how it is accounted for and regulated.

entries.text: Arinze sells cars for dealers on commission and flips her first vehicle with the proceeds. Autogirl is formally registered in 2019 as a dealership and rental business.
Pivot to peer-to-peer rentals, run on calls, WhatsApp and Google Sheets. By June 2022, revenue covers payroll for seven staff with no outside investor; a first seed round is planned.
Around 3,000 trips completed and roughly 123 corporate clients served. Free driver-training programme for women launched.

Operations rebuilt as the Muvment platform with live booking and owner dashboards. 12,000+ rides; $530,000+ paid to owners (TechCabal, January 2026). $2,000 UpGreyed Her grant (May); Ghana launch (June); GET Accelerated 2024 cohort; Seedstars accelerator.
Named one of five GET Accelerated startups to receive an additional ₦10M in equity-free funding.

Absorbs a ₦20M (~$14,000) loss on an uninsured self-drive crash; makes verified comprehensive insurance a listing condition (TechCabal, January 2026). Targets Ghana profitability in 2026, eyes Kenya, Côte d’Ivoire and Benin, and lists electric vehicles.

Prado investment offer reported, built around Autogirl’s strongest rental category. Company marketing says a Prado can earn about ₦100,000 a day and up to ₦30M a year in gross rental income; the source does not state occupancy, costs or contractual terms (Muvment by Autogirl, July 2026).
